# Using Meld for Diffs {#sec-meld-difftool}

The lessons show differences between versions of a file with `git diff`, which prints its output right in the terminal. That is quick for a line or two, but hard to read once changes get larger. [Meld]{.uwred} is a free, graphical diff tool that shows the two versions [side by side]{.uwred}, with changes highlighted and lined up — much easier to scan than terminal output.

This appendix installs Meld and sets it up as Git's default [difftool]{.uwred}, so you can open any `git diff` in Meld instead. It is optional but recommended. Plan on about ten minutes.

::: {.callout-note}
Meld opens a graphical window, so it only works where you have a desktop. On a headless server or a terminal-only remote session, keep using plain `git diff`.
:::

## Step 1: Install Meld

Pick the instructions for your operating system, then confirm the install at the end.

### Windows

Download the installer from [meldmerge.org](https://meldmerge.org/) and run it. You can accept the [defaults]{.uwred} on every screen. The installer adds Meld to your `PATH` so that Git Bash can find it.

### macOS

The simplest route is [Homebrew](https://brew.sh/):

```bash
brew install --cask meld
```

If you do not use Homebrew, download the `.dmg` from [meldmerge.org](https://meldmerge.org/) and drag Meld into your Applications folder. (With the `.dmg` route, the `meld` command may not be on your `PATH`; Homebrew sets that up for you, which is why it is the easier option here.)

### Linux

Install from your distribution's package manager:

```bash
# Debian / Ubuntu
sudo apt install meld

# Fedora
sudo dnf install meld
```

### Confirm it worked

In your terminal (Git Bash on Windows), check that Meld is on your `PATH`:

```bash
meld --version
```

```
meld 3.22.0
```

A version number means Git will be able to launch it.

## Step 2: Set Meld as Git's difftool

Tell Git to use Meld whenever you run `git difftool`. These three commands write the settings to your global Git configuration, so you only do this [once per computer]{.uwred}:

```bash
git config --global diff.tool meld
git config --global difftool.prompt false
git config --global difftool.meld.cmd 'meld "$LOCAL" "$REMOTE"'
```

- [`diff.tool meld`]{.uwred} makes Meld the default difftool.
- [`difftool.prompt false`]{.uwred} skips the "Launch meld?" confirmation before each file.
- [`difftool.meld.cmd`]{.uwred} tells Git how to call Meld, with the two versions as its panes.

::: {.callout-note}
Use [single quotes]{.uwred} around the `cmd` value. They keep `$LOCAL` and `$REMOTE` as literal text in your config file — Git fills them in with the actual file versions each time it runs.
:::

These commands edit the `.gitconfig` file in your home folder. If you prefer to edit it by hand, the equivalent block is:

```
[diff]
    tool = meld
[difftool]
    prompt = false
[difftool "meld"]
    cmd = meld "$LOCAL" "$REMOTE"
```

## Step 3: Use it

Anywhere the lessons use `git diff`, you can swap in [`git difftool`]{.uwred} to open the comparison in Meld instead:

| Command | What Meld shows |
|---|---|
| `git difftool <file>` | Your uncommitted copy vs. the last commit |
| `git difftool <commit> <file>` | A past version vs. your current copy |
| `git difftool HEAD HEAD~2 <file>` | The latest commit vs. two commits back |
| `git difftool <hash1> <hash2> <file>` | Two specific past versions, side by side |

Meld opens a window with the two versions aligned. Close the window to return to the terminal; with `difftool.prompt false` set, Git moves on to the next file (if any) on its own.

Meld is also handy on its own, outside of Git: launch it and pick any two files to compare — for example, a document in your repo against an edited copy a collaborator emailed you.

## Optional: use Meld to resolve merge conflicts

Meld can also help with the merge conflicts from the [Conflicts]{.uwred} unit, showing your version, the incoming version, and the merged result together. To set it up as Git's [mergetool]{.uwred}:

```bash
git config --global merge.tool meld
git config --global mergetool.prompt false
git config --global mergetool.meld.cmd 'meld "$LOCAL" "$MERGED" "$REMOTE" --output "$MERGED"'
```

Then, when a `git pull` or `git merge` reports a conflict, run:

```bash
git mergetool
```

Meld opens with the merged file in the center pane. Edit it until it reads how you want, save, and close. Then finish the merge the usual way with `git add` and `git commit`.
